pages.title: What makes a boat a boat?
pages.text: Boats can look very different. But every boat must float and support its load.
pages.question: What does a boat actually need to do?

pages.title: Start with what matters
pages.text: Imagine a boat with no motor, no sail and no paint.
pages.question: Could it still float? Which parts are essential?

pages.title: Design a floating boat
pages.text: Change the space inside the hull and the weight of its cargo.
pages.question: Can you make a boat that floats with more cargo?

pages.title: Build from basic facts
pages.text: First principles thinking means identifying the basic facts and constraints of a problem, then reasoning from them instead of copying an existing solution.
pages.question: What fact about floating did your design depend on?

pages.title: Rethink a chair
pages.text: A chair does not have to have four legs. It needs to support a person safely.
pages.question: Draw three different chairs that solve the same problem.

pages.title: A guess is not a fact
pages.text: Someone says that every heavy object falls faster than a light one.
pages.question: How could you find out?

pages.title: Make a prediction
pages.text: Imagine dropping two balls of the same size and shape but different weights. Ignore air resistance.
pages.question: Which ball will reach the ground first?

pages.title: Drop two balls
pages.text: Choose their masses and release them together.
pages.question: Does changing their mass change the time to land in this model?

pages.title: Look for a way to be wrong
pages.text: A testable idea makes a prediction that evidence could contradict. In this ideal model, gravity gives both balls the same acceleration.
pages.question: What observation would contradict the original claim?

pages.title: Try it outside
pages.text: With an adult, drop two safe, similar-sized balls from the same low height onto a clear surface.
pages.question: What would you change to make the comparison fair?

pages.title: Nobody is in charge
pages.text: A flock of birds can turn together even though no single bird controls the whole flock.
pages.question: How could thousands of birds coordinate?

pages.title: A few simple rules
pages.text: Imagine each bird avoids collisions, moves toward nearby birds and copies their direction.
pages.question: What might happen when every bird follows those rules?

pages.title: Make a flock
pages.text: Switch between independent movement and neighbour rules. Watch the group change.
pages.question: Did you tell each bird where to fly?

pages.title: A pattern emerges
pages.text: Emergence is when interactions between parts create a pattern at the scale of the whole system. No bird needs to know the shape of the flock.
pages.question: Can you describe the difference between an individual bird and the group?

pages.title: Look for patterns
pages.text: Observe a group of birds, ants or people. Look for patterns in how they move or respond to each other.
pages.question: What simple rules might help explain the pattern?

pages.title: A change causes another change
pages.text: When a room becomes cold, a thermostat can switch a heater on. When the room warms up, it switches it off.
pages.question: Why does the heater not need to stay on forever?

pages.title: Keep a room comfortable
pages.text: Imagine a heater that never checks the temperature.
pages.question: What would happen if it kept heating?

pages.title: Control the temperature
pages.text: Turn feedback on or off, change the target temperature, then advance time.
pages.question: Which rule keeps the room closer to the target?

pages.title: Feedback changes behaviour
pages.text: Negative feedback counteracts a change. Positive feedback amplifies a change. A thermostat uses negative feedback to keep temperature near its target.
pages.question: How does the heater respond to its own effect?

pages.title: Find a feedback loop
pages.text: Think about being hungry, eating and becoming full.
pages.question: How does feeling full change what you do next?

pages.title: Connected things
pages.text: Roads connect towns. Messages travel between people. Roots and fungi can form networks in soil.
pages.question: What can a connection allow to move?

pages.title: A broken connection
pages.text: Imagine a road between two towns is blocked.
pages.question: What happens if there is another road? What if there is not?

pages.title: Build a route
pages.text: Tap connections to open or close roads. Try to keep the start connected to the destination.
pages.question: Can you make two independent routes?

pages.title: Connections matter
pages.text: A network consists of nodes and links. Its structure affects how things can move, how easily failures spread and whether alternate paths exist.
pages.question: Which connections are most important in your network?

pages.title: Map your neighbourhood
pages.text: Draw your home and three nearby places. Connect them with roads or paths.
pages.question: Can you reach the same place in more than one way?

pages.title: One becomes two
pages.text: Imagine a pond with one lily pad. Every day each lily pad produces one more.
pages.question: How many will there be tomorrow?

pages.title: How fast does it grow?
pages.text: The number doubles each day, as long as there is enough space and resources.
pages.question: Will the pond fill slowly all the way to the end?

pages.title: Grow the pond
pages.text: Move through the days and watch the number of lily pads double.
pages.question: If the pond is full on day seven, when was it half full?

pages.title: Growth builds on growth
pages.text: Exponential growth happens when a quantity increases by the same proportion over equal intervals. The amount added gets larger as the total grows.
pages.question: Why is the last day's increase much larger than the first day's?

pages.title: Fold and double
pages.text: Draw one dot, then two, then four, then eight. Continue on paper.
pages.question: How many dots would you need after ten doublings?

pages.title: You cannot do everything
pages.text: Imagine you have six wooden blocks. You want to build a house, a bridge and a boat.
pages.question: Can you use the same block in two places at once?

pages.title: Choose what matters
pages.text: A house might need three blocks. A bridge might need three, too.
pages.question: What happens to the boat if you build both?

pages.title: Allocate your materials
pages.text: Distribute six blocks among three projects. Take blocks back to change your plan.
pages.question: What did you give up by choosing one project?

pages.title: Every choice has a cost
pages.text: Scarcity means resources are limited relative to possible uses. Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you give up when you choose.
pages.question: What is the next-best use of your blocks?

pages.title: Plan an afternoon
pages.text: You have one hour. You want to read, build something and go outside.
pages.question: How would you use your time, and what would you give up?

pages.title: Better in one way
pages.text: A bicycle with a very light frame is easier to carry. A stronger frame might weigh more.
pages.question: Can a design be best at everything?

pages.title: Choose a design goal
pages.text: Imagine you need to carry a heavy load, or travel as quickly as possible.
pages.question: Would you choose the same design for both jobs?

pages.title: Design a vehicle
pages.text: Add reinforcement to a simple model. It increases strength but also adds weight.
pages.question: Which design suits a heavy load? Which is easiest to carry?

pages.title: Trade-offs
pages.text: A trade-off occurs when improving one property comes at the cost of another under a constraint. The right design depends on what you value and need.
pages.question: Why is there no single best design for every job?

pages.title: Look at your own boat
pages.text: Think of a wide stable hull and a narrow hull that may move through water more easily.
pages.question: Which would you choose for cargo, and which for a race?
